en: Preface to the *Śīlaskandha-sūtra*, composed by Daoyan of Yingjiang. Regarding the title of this preface:
in general, the establishment of titles is intended to preserve brevity and avoid redundancy, so that when one opens the scroll, the meaning is easily understood, and doubts are forever eliminated.

This present title briefly clarifies three distinctions. Regarding the term "four divisions" (*caturvarga*): it is a specific name for one of the five schools and a general designation for this single tradition.
Since each of the various schools possesses its own *Prātimokṣa*, this term is specifically cited here to distinguish it from other traditions. Regarding the term "bhikṣu":

although there was also a commentary on the *Prātimokṣa* for bhikṣuṇīs, that text has already been lost. Regarding the phrase "including the commentary": [it refers to the fact that] the commentary is contained within [the root text].
Having simplified the differences and edited the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*, I have transcribed the original text for the sake of public recitation.

Now, I have privately extracted the commentary from the extensive *Vinaya* to annotate this authentic scripture, so that the principles of the precepts may be clearly understood and the distinctions between observance and violation easily recognized; hence it is called the "Annotated Prātimokṣa.

Regarding the term "Prātimokṣa," the sub-commentary states: "It reveals the essence of the teaching. "Precept" (*śīla*) means to prohibit and to warn; it is the fundamental cause and basis of all practices.
This refers to the "roots" (indriya). Because they can generate and bring about the tasks of the Path, this precept is the foundation of the Path;

furthermore, the precept is the foundation of practice, for both mundane and supramundane practices rely upon it. Moreover, the precept is the foundation of the teaching; the extensive Vinaya-piṭaka is merely an explanation of the text concerning preceptual conduct, and thus it should properly be called the *Vinaya-mūla* (Root of the Vinaya);
what we now cite as the headings of the practice is the teaching itself. It is also said that the precept is the "exposition."

The original text in the *Zàjìquàn yǒusīyīchéng wén* states: "Those who come from within the *Poṣadha-sūtra* recited every half-month—does this not mean that what is preached serves as the basis for the transmitter?
Furthermore, it says that for the listener, the preaching is the basis; they listen with their ears and receive it with their minds, seeking out the preaching to give rise to practice.
The preceding two points explain this by way of the *dharmas* being signified (*saṃgṛhīta-dharma*), while the subsequent three points relate to... [the subject of the practitioner].
Regarding the term "preface" (*xu*) used to denote the explanatory text: the *Erya* states that the east and west walls are called "prefaces.
Just as the walls of a house stand outside the main hall and inner sanctum, this metaphor illustrates how the preface stands at the forefront of an entire scripture.
Regarding Mount Taiyi, ancient texts identify it as Zhongnan; thus, these two names are both common designations for the same mountain.
Some have doubted this, suggesting that Taiyi refers to a specific peak. As for the term "śramaṇa," it is a Sanskrit word (*śramaṇa*);

translated here as "diligent cessation," it means to diligently practice all forms of goodness and to cease all evils. The *Sūtra in Forty-two Sections* states: "Leaving one's kin to enter the homeless life, one attains realization..."
When the mind reaches the fundamental understanding that unconditioned dharmas (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) are its true nature, it is called a *śramaṇa*.

Furthermore, regarding the designation "Śākya," those in the Western lands who follow non-Buddhist paths generally refer to all who have left the household life as *śramaṇas*. Here, we specifically designate the Śākya clan to preserve the distinction [between Buddhists and others].
This account follows the established precedent of former scholars and is composed as a formal exposition.
In the first section of the preface, the opening phrase sets forth the core tenets of the teaching; the following two phrases praise the preceding title by citing cause and effect.

Regarding the term "ten thousand practices" (*sahasra-caryā*), there are two interpretations. If understood according to the Vinaya (the *śikṣāpada*), this *Prātimokṣa* Sūtra encompasses both wholesome and unwholesome matters and phenomena to correspond to the two types of practice:
cessation and performance. "Cessation practice" refers to the abandonment of evil, while "performance practice" refers to the cultivation of goodness.
Although the paths of practice are many, none transcend these two. Furthermore, if we speak in terms of their objects, the precepts are immeasurable;

yet, by listing the two hundred and fifty rules as the pathways for upholding and violating them, one understands that the scriptural texts encompass all aspects. As the Sūtra says: "If there were further Buddha-dharmas, how could they not be included?
Next, regarding the explanation of the *āgama* (direct) and *upadeśa* (transformative) teachings on various practices: if they are not [contained within] this...

If preceptual conduct (*śīla*) is impure, giving (*dāna*) is not pure; if diligence (*vīrya*), patience (*kṣānti*), meditation (*dhyāna*), and wisdom (*prajñā*) are merely suffering, then the myriad practices will not arise and the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*) will not emerge.

Since the six perfections must take precepts as their foundation, the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* states: "The pavilion of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*) takes precepts as its pillars; the city of the meditative mind takes precepts as its walls.
Because this text explains precepts, we know they comprehensively encompass all practices, both mundane and supramundane. As the *Sūtra Commentary* says: "Mundane and supramundane practices..."

Following the aforementioned statement, "thorough thoroughfare" (tongqu) refers to a four-way road; this serves as a metaphor for this precept, which gives rise to the myriad practices (*sahasra-pratipatti*) such that there is nowhere it does not penetrate.
Thus, the *Chao* states: "In aspiring toward the myriad practices, the precepts serve as the sovereign lord. The *Shu* states:
"That which the myriad practices rely upon must depend on the precepts to be established."

The second phrase clarifies the fruit. "The Three Vehicles" refers to those who can ride—the Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Buddhas—and the vehicles upon which they ride—the Four Noble Truths, the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination, and the Six Perfections.
It takes the sense of "transporting" as its meaning; that is to say, there are no holy persons whatsoever who do not take the precepts as their initial gateway.
Regarding the term "correct track" (*zhenggui*): "correct" (*zheng*) serves to exclude what is erroneous, while "track" (*gui*) refers to the ruts of a carriage. By means of...

The preceding section opens the thoroughfare of the myriad practices and leads one into the tracks of the Three Vehicles; thus, the two meanings of cause and effect are made increasingly clear herein.
Nevertheless, the Patriarchs’ compositions are vast in their sublime wisdom, often exhausting the intent of an entire sutra with only a few phrases.

Now, regarding the praise for the precepts, although the text consists of only two sentences, the teaching of cause and effect and the conclusion of the praise for practice are fully contained therein; this is indeed a concise summary.
To speak of the general outline, its essential principles do not exceed these points.

In the "Arousing of Zeal," there are two parts. First, a general discussion on the conditions for worldly transcendence; the first line describes the Dharma King who has transcended the world, referring specifically to the Tathāgata.
As the Sūtra says: "I am the Dharma King, sovereign over the Dharma. The phrase "benefiting those who see" is derived from the *Book of Changes* (Zhouyi), in the section on Qian.

In the hexagram, both the second and fifth lines state, "It is advantageous to see the Great Man. This clarifies that when a sovereign emerges from concealment and ascends to the throne, he must accord with the hearts of the age, and all things should observe him.
Now, it is said that the Tathāgata, riding upon the occasion and responding to the world, has matured the conditions for sentient beings; thus they should behold him.

Therefore, the words of that hexagram are borrowed to clarify his manifestation in the world. The subsequent phrase clarifies the benefit to those with the capacity [for awakening], meaning the establishment of the teaching and its opening.

Since every variety of expedient means is employed for the sake of sentient beings, it is said that "it exists in dependence on conditions"; these conditions are precisely the spiritual capacities [of those to be saved].
Alternatively, it may be understood that whatever is propagated and elucidated does not arise in isolation, but must rely upon causes and conditions to serve as its point of inception.
Section Six: Correctly Demonstrating the Arising of Zeal, Part Two. First, an account of the compassionate mind regarding all beings.

As for the statement that "the Sages were grieved and distressed," according to the *Prātimokṣa-vinaya-kaṇḍa*: at that time, the World-Honored One was dwelling in a quiet place, reflecting and thinking:
"I have established the recitation of the *Prātimokṣa* for the bhikṣus; among them are faithful bhikṣus who have newly received the precepts."
"Having not heard the precepts and not knowing how they should be studied, I think it would be better for me now to listen as the bhikṣus gather in one place to recite the precepts.
At that time, the World-Honored One emerged from his secluded dwelling and, on account of this matter, assembled the bhikṣus and addressed them, saying:
"...down to: 'Gather together in one place. Regarding the recitation of the precepts, speak thus: 'Venerable sirs, I now wish...'"
The *Prātimokṣa* has been explained (the above is from the Vinaya text). Now, "the former sages" refers specifically to the Tathāgata.

This is because, while contemplating in a secluded place, his noble mind was filled with profound sorrow as he took pity on those newly initiated in their studies; thus it is said he was "mournful and anxious. These words appear in the *Wenxuan*:

"In the governance of the sage-philosophers, they were mournful and anxious; Confucius' mat was not warm for long, and the soot on Mozi's wall was not yet black. This refers to such sage-philosophers.
Practicing the Way and governing the world, one constantly laments that the times are not yet saved; thus Confucius’s seat was never warm and his bed never settled.
Mo Di did not even have time to eat a full meal because he was not dark-skinned enough [to be a slave]. Now, borrowing their words, the intent seems similar to what Cheng You has shown:

the term "small ordinary" (xiaofan) generally encompasses both internal and external thin stages (*mṛdu-bhūmi*). However, if one follows the meaning of the preceding Vinaya rules, it specifically refers to those who have newly received the precepts.

"Precepts" (*śīla*) refers to "sinking and drowning," meaning that through ignorance of the characteristics of the precepts, one may commit transgressions and fall into the evil destinies. "Lamenting" (*dāu*) refers to sorrowful sighing.

Therefore, the following section clarifies the establishment of teachings according to the capacities of beings. The first two phrases describe the gate of not shying away from the formalization of the precepts; "gate" (*mōn*) here refers specifically to the precepts.

In the Vinaya, "to avoid" (huì) means "to conceal faults. Since the precepts established by the Tathāgata all point out the coarse evils and afflictions of sentient beings—extending from the characteristics of lust and theft to various types of unwholesome karma—they reveal these faults so that people may know them and distance themselves from them;
therefore, it is said that they do not "avoid" [them]. "Pí" means "to open. As for "secret arts," these disciplinary laws are intended solely for those within [the Sangha].
Because the laity and the other four assemblies were not permitted to hear it, the *Shuochao* (Commentary) quotes a treatise, asking:
"Why was the Vinaya included at the first council? Because it is secret and sublime. Furthermore, the *Fenbie Gongde Lun* (Treatise on the Distinction of Merits) states:
"Because it is supremely esoteric, it is not seen by worldly people. "Shu" refers to the Way or arts; alternatively, the pronunciation is "sui," meaning a path or road.
Zhang next clarifies the regulations for preaching, which consists of three parts. First, he shows the original intent behind establishing these regulations.

Regarding the "unprompted preaching," it is because when the Tathāgata preached the Dharma, he invariably required a question as a prelude; yet this regulation for preaching the precepts involves contemplating in a quiet place and self-restraint through the holy mind.
Thus, his great compassion is keenly directed toward the conditions of sentient beings, and he deeply considers that those who are newly learning the path may not understand the precepts.
Regarding the arising of conflicting precepts, because it is not intentional, one restrains oneself without waiting for a question; this teaching reveals how a beginner should train.

As previously cited, for one newly receiving the precepts, it is said: "How should one study the Vinaya? This refers to making known the characteristics of the precepts so that they may be upheld and observed.

This applies equally to those who practice in seclusion. Furthermore, as indicated by the source of the teaching previously cited, the "one dharma of reciting the precepts" (Uposatha) involves the assembly of the community and so forth.
The previously cited Vinaya text states: "At that time, the World-Honored One emerged from his secluded dwelling and, for this reason, assembled [the monks] in one place.
Here, Xuánfàn points directly to the Dharma of the precepts.

The preceding section (1) indicates the scriptural standard of the teaching; according to the commentary’s analysis, the sutra is divided into three major sections, and the first two phrases of the current text [correspond to the first].
Then, at the beginning of the preface, the verses beginning with "I bow my head" (*pūrvam praṇipatya*) and so forth were presented;

Dharmarakṣa’s compilation provides a general introduction to both the extensive and abbreviated teachings, establishing the foundation for exposition and listening through the preceding remarks on upholding and violating [the precepts]. Following this, the Buddha himself arranged the subsequent sections as the main body (*samyak-siddhānta*), which serves as the origin of the causal conditions.
The next two lines specifically point to the main body by means of the items listed in the *Piñjū* (sections on training rules).

The various rules regarding the gravity of offenses, their observance or violation, their allowance or prohibition, and the prevention of transgressions are arrayed like a net to regulate the faculties and desires [of practitioners].
Regarding the following three sections, which describe the meaning of the speaker, there are four points: first, determining the time of the teaching;

second, enjoining the assembly to gather; third, selecting the audience; and fourth, manifesting the benefits. First, concerning the time, according to the Vinaya, it was due to certain non-Buddhist brahmins...
On the eighth, fourteenth, and fifteenth days of the month, the assembly gathered at these three times, coming and going and circulating together as companions.

They provided one another with food and drink, cherished each other deeply, and made offerings day after day. At that time, King Bimbisāra, having witnessed this occurrence, went one day to inform the Buddha.
It was then that the Buddha first instructed the bhikṣus to assemble for the three times of the month to preach the Dharma and discuss its meaning. This was the beginning of this practice.

Originally, the rule for reciting the *Prātimokṣa* had not yet been established. Later, while the Tathāgata was reflecting in seclusion, he instituted this regulation; at first, the *Poṣadha* was to be recited every day.

Because the assembly became exhausted, it was subsequently regulated to be held every half-month. The *Shu* (Commentary) states: "Therefore, it is based on the new and full moon as a convenient midpoint.

Next, the regulation for assembling [the Sangha] was established. The *Shu* states: "Since these are all the same correct precepts, they are what the assembly collectively hears; it is only right that they be revered and observed."
There must be no discord or separation; as originally established by the Vinaya, the entire Jambudvīpa was naturally unified into a single assembly.
Later, because traveling long distances impaired the Path, it was opened up to four locations with six characteristics, eventually becoming restricted to specific places.

Nevertheless, when it comes to the time for reciting the precepts (*poṣadha*), there is no restriction as to whether one is inside or outside the boundary; all must assemble together. To distinguish this from other gatherings, the Vinaya states:

One who has committed an offense may not hear the precepts, nor may one preach them to an offender; therefore, the Commentary states: "In general, those who wish to hear the precepts must be persons whose conduct is pure (*śuddhacārin*);
if there is a transgression, it contravenes the method for reciting the precepts. *He* (合) means "appropriate"; *jie* (潔) means "pure conduct" and so forth;
*you* (猶) means "the same as. Regarding the benefit of manifestation, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* asks: "For how long will the Buddha-dharma abide in the world?"
The Buddha replied: "Because the precepts are recited according to the purity of the bhikṣus, and because those whose names are not corrupted shall abide in the world.

The commentary states: "This is truly because, upon hearing the teachings once, they are practiced with faith and obedience; their karma does not incline inwardly [toward defilement], and concentration and wisdom arise within them.

Thus, the two fruits—both distant and proximate—are produced through inconceivable power, leading future generations and perpetually sustaining the Dharma for ten thousand years; therefore, it is said that the Dharma abides for a long time."

Regarding the initial section of the transmission in both lands, it is first divided into three parts. First, the description of the shifting of time and the transformation of conditions is further divided into two. The first two phrases clarify the passage of time;

the upper phrase describes time, stating that "the [teachings] do not compete," because the periods of the True Dharma (*saddharma*), the Semblance Dharma (*pratirūpaka-dharma*), and the Final Dharma (*paścima-dharma*) necessarily follow one another in sequence and cannot arrive simultaneously—"compete" here meaning "to occur concurrently.
The lower phrase describes conditions, stating that they "flow and transform," meaning that sometimes the essence is pure at first and becomes diluted later, or...
As faculties differ—whether sharp or dull—and as attachments and views diverge, the inclinations of beings vary accordingly. The second couplet cites scriptural evidence for the preceding line:
the first part refers to the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra*, concerning the dream of an elder of a single bolt of wool that subsequently became five segments;

the Buddha declared, "After my parinirvāṇa, there will be disciples who divide into five schools," and so forth. The latter part refers to the present Vinaya, concerning the dispute among the monks of Kauśāmbī.
When he arrived at Śrāvastī, the various upāsakas asked the Buddha how they should practice giving. The Buddha said:
"It should be divided into two portions; for this [recipient] is the Saṃgha, and that [recipient] is also the Saṃgha—just as when a golden staff is divided into two parts, both are gold."
Regarding the next section on the branches of the teachings for future clarification: the first phrase refers to the teachings as the means of expression (*vyañjana*).

This refers to the fact that each school arose through its own compilation; as the *Shu-chao* states: "According to their respective inclinations, they established their own tenets, competing for brilliance, such that the great assemblies each gave rise to divergent attachments.

As the *Shu-chao* further states: "It was simply because the capacities and awakenings [of sentient beings] differed that the various schools were established. The second phrase refers to the two categories of the provisional and the ultimate.

That is to say, the four stages are divided into departments as explained in the *Shuji* (Commentary): the metaphor of "clouds flying" illustrates their dispersal, while the metaphor of "mountains spreading" illustrates their stubborn adherence.

Regarding the three [stages] below, they represent the Tathāgata’s far-reaching influence; regarding the two lines above, they mean that [the teaching] universally encompasses all speculative views, as the precepts were first established.
Thus there are ten thousand differences, which arise precisely because the faculties and capacities (*indriya*) of sentient beings vary and their inclinations toward what they wish to hear differ;

therefore, the Sage established varying degrees of gravity and distinct priorities of urgency across the various schools. The relative weight of these schools is indeed immeasurable. The latter two lines mean that all ultimately return to the primary practice (*samyak-karman*);
for although the various schools are divided and their perspectives differ, when it comes to destroying delusions and elucidating the ultimate goal, they are one.
Because the fruits differ, the *Mahāsaṃnipāta-sūtra* states that although the five schools differ, they do not obstruct the Buddha-dharmadhātu or nirvāṇa.

In the first section of the "Ancient Traditions" (*Xichuan*) recorded in the *Donghua*, there are three parts: first, it marks the beginning and end of the transmission and compilation; second, according to the *Sifen-jieben*, this corresponds to the initial translation of the golden words by Jueming of the Yao Qin dynasty when he recited the Vinaya;

as for those of the Cao Wei, they are... [text ends]... (Note: The provided source text appears to be a fragment of a Buddhist historical or bibliographical commentary. The translation reflects the available portion.)

Because Dharmakāla first received the ritual for ordination (*upasampadā*) from the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya-citta*, it is said that [the Vinaya] was "first transmitted. Thus, the *Xian-ding xu* (Preface to the Compiled Version) states:
"Since the practice of the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* reached the land of Dongxia (China), during the middle period of the Cao Wei dynasty, Dharmarakṣa first transmitted the *Karmavācanā*;

however, while the *Karmavācanā* clarifies the *Prātimokṣa*, the latter remains incomplete. Furthermore, as the *Śāstra* says: "From the beginning of Emperor Ming of Han’s dream... and so forth, referring to Kāśyapa Mātanga and Dharmaratna.

Since the transmission of the Dharma began, the foundations were merely being laid and there had not yet been time to establish concrete forms; for over two hundred years, neither the monastic community nor the laity had received the precepts of taking refuge.

During the Jiaping era (the reign of the fourth sovereign) of the Wei dynasty, the Indian śramaṇa Dharmakāla (translated into Chinese as Fashi) arrived and established the *Mahāsāṃghika-śīla-hṛdaya* (The Heart of the Mahāsāṃghika Precepts), whereby the formal *karmavācanā* for full ordination was finally instituted.
In the first year of the Zhengyuan era of the Most Noble Prince (the Fifth Lord), the Anxi śramaṇa Tandi produced the *Karmavācanā* of the Mahīśāsaka school.
These two schools were initially located in Luoyang; this is what is called the beginning of the Vinaya.
"At the commencement of the Sui dynasty" refers to the time of Emperor Wen; it means that the *Prātimokṣasūtra* began at the end of the Wei period and continued until the beginning of the Sui.
Throughout the course of its transmission, there have been not a few instances of excision, alteration, and displacement.
Second, in the following list presented within the main text, the "four versions" refers to four distinct recensions; the details are clearly revealed in the text as explained below.
Regarding the term "clerical script" (*lìwén*), there are two interpretations: one suggests it refers to the scribes who transcribed those original texts into this clerical style.
These characters were used for this concise and archaic script; it originated in the time of Fuxi when the historian Cangjie observed bird tracks to create writing.
Later, Cheng Miao simplified the seal script (*zhuanshu*) into the clerical script (*lishu*), which is precisely what we now call *zong*.

Some say that "clerical" (*li*) is an error for "clerical-style" (*lishu*). The subsequent phrase, "according to the regulations, one may be included among those who take refuge," refers to the transcription of the legal text alone.

Regarding the third instance of "讎" (chóu): the latter part generally assigns the fault of error to the proofreading, while the first two phrases clarify that it was not a matter of collation. The commentary on the *Zhuàn* of the *Zuǒzhuan* states:

"Chóu means 'to correspond' (*duì*). This refers to comparing various editions; because their textual meanings were pruned or altered such that the underlying principles became contradictory, those who relied upon and upheld them could not understand the phenomena [of the text], hence it is said they were 'obscured' (*méngrán*).
The *Zhòuyī* says: 'A spring emerging from beneath a mountain is called *móng*'. This is because...

The two lines following "has not yet reached" clarify the loss [of the original] mentioned in the preceding line: the first line means that the sages deceive the worthy, while the second line means they obstruct and block those who come to study.

Separately clarifying the internal text, there are eight lines that meticulously distinguish the gains and losses of the four versions; however, the first version is entirely lost, while the remaining three possess both gains and losses.
Furthermore, the phrase "the Sanskrit version" refers to those instances where the text is largely expanded in the upper line and then sublated and refuted in the lower line.
The Sanskrit terminology has caused confusion regarding the textual meaning, such that the respective dialects and significations do not harmonize.
According to the Vinaya, those who merely transcribe the characters in clerical script (*lishu*) are said to "take refuge" in the sense that they understand the fundamental principles;

those who "discern the characteristics" are said to mean there are no further commentaries, as they simply transcribe the text of the precepts so that the distinctions between grave and light offenses remain obscure and indistinguishable. As for Huigou, he is identified as Master Huiguang, who stated that—

Because he sought the textual characteristics through their underlying principles, the Preface to the Commentary states: "Following the meaning and summarizing the text. Furthermore, the Preface to the Revised Edition states:

"Again, seeking through the meaning, I have compiled what was omitted and lost to illuminate the Master’s composition. Thus, the *Guanglü shu*, the *Jiemo*, and the *Jieben* were all revised in accordance with this principle, deeply harmonizing with the meaning.
As for the breadth of his vision, it has not yet been settled; regarding the points of debate, it is said that successive challenges and difficulties have not yet reached a conclusion.
"Exhausting the Principle" refers to what is stated in the preface: "The principles of the school produced by this humble light clarify the text.
"Relying on Conditions" refers to what was produced by Vinaya Master Fǎyuàn; that is, relying on the Vinaya to cite conditions as the primary authority. Thus, the preface to the *Śāstra* says:

"Reciting the Vinaya and calculating its texts, I have edited and finalized the preface," and the preface text says: "In accordance with the Vinaya-piṭaka, I have transcribed the core of the precepts. This is complete.
It is as if one were to see things in detail and distinction, yet claim that this is merely the plan of a single family, which cannot be universally applied to the minds of all beings.

In the general critique, there are three parts: first, citing the holy ones' direct formulation of the authentic precepts; second, clarifying that the noble path of renunciation is not comparable to heterodox arts;

and third, explaining that the prohibitions are intended to awaken the mind against falsehood and that their meaning is not obscure—therefore, these were formulated by the Buddha alone, based on both the sūtras and the śāstras.
While other studies may be common to other sages, this Vinaya alone was personally proclaimed by the Buddha’s own golden mouth.

This is because within the Great Trichiliocosm, the Buddha is the Dharma King, and the Vinaya is his royal decree; it was established solely by the Sage. All others of lower status may only rely upon and uphold it.

It is like a state where rewards and punishments, as well as edicts and commands, issue from the Queen; if a subject presumes to issue them, he is but a commoner who loses his credibility and perishes.

There will be no day of defeat; the Dharma of the precepts is likewise. If one examines the official teachings, it is said that if sentient beings do not uphold the Dharma, they will not abide for long.

That the worthy and sages reverently uphold it is precisely because the Tathāgata’s practice has reached its ultimate fruit and his realization is perfect and exhaustive regarding the heavy and light karmic natures of sentient beings.
Even those below him cannot bear [to disparage it], let alone other minor sages who would dare to speculate upon it? They remain silent, as if it did not exist.
I venture to set forth these words in humble reverence, having received and inherited your strict instructions.

Therefore, the following two sections discuss the "Patriarchal Scriptures" (*zongjing*). "Patriarchal Scriptures" refers to those treatises that explain the Vinaya-piṭaka by taking the fundamental teachings of the Sūtras as their primary authority, without deviating from the original intent of the scriptures.
Regarding this, there are two interpretations: one based on the distinction between the Great and Small Vehicles, and the other based on the distinction between the noble and the ordinary.

It is said that because our assigned positions have not yet fully exhausted the Sage’s intent, we speak of "conjecture. Alternatively, when explaining by summarizing the treatises, if the interpretation does not accord with the text, one must not conflate it with the Buddha’s words.
One should distinguish the sections and append the commentary to the Sage’s intent, never daring to speculate or recklessly deviate from it;

hence the *Shu* (Commentary) says: "The five divisions and eighteen schools are merely human classifications; as for the Vinaya teachings, there is nothing that is not the Sage’s own purport. What [of yours] is not so?

This refers to those who, having attained the state of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), yet dare to employ erroneous language; even if they possess some understanding, they compile it into their own volumes.

Generally, the following three lines directly rebuke errors and delusions. The first two lines point to and rebuke various views; the preceding sections refer to the emotional attachments and arbitrary opinions of various previous versions, which are called "delusions" because they follow one's own whims.
An example is: "To establish what was not prescribed as prescribed, and to violate what was prescribed"—this is what is meant. Below this...

The two phrases reveal the brevity [of this work]. That is to say, upon carefully examining the ancients, it was found that for the most part there was no practical benefit; thus, to recount them would have been useless, which is why it is said, "I have not had the leisure.

Now, at the beginning of this compilation, the section is divided into two parts. First, the initial two phrases of the preceding section refute the redundancy of the ancient texts, asserting that while the words may be numerous, the meaning sought therein is what truly matters.

The reasons for this abbreviation lie in the fact that the Sanskrit original was written in *lipi* script; however, its meaning is obscured and its principles flow into obscurity because the text is restricted and congested.

Alternatively, it may be that all four versions possess various faults: the first two lines reveal the deficiency in the ritual application and the loss of proper decorum, as the ritual procedures are incomplete;
the latter two lines reveal the lack of authoritative basis, as there is no formal record for their observance.
If the latter two lines clarify the present, the first line refers to the composition of this collection, while the second line means that it is easy for later students to understand. Alternatively,
the first line may refer to the characteristics of errors in various ancient texts, and the second line means that once past mistakes have been exposed,
one then admires the later teachings.

In the subsequent section explaining the stages of study (*śikṣā-bhūmi*), there are three parts; the first two lines describe his early aspirations. The first line refers to his longing for the Way, while the remainder explains how he was instructed by me:
"Those who look up [to the Dharma] from a young age" refers to the fact that the Patriarch left home at the age of seven and received full ordination upon reaching adulthood.

The commentary on the *Śāstra* states: "In the past, while still a child, he possessed faith; having no opportunity to be led away [by worldly ties], he reached the age beyond childhood, ten years old."

There are five points: first, seeking out a teacher; second, reciting the scriptures sixteen times; third, shaving the head; fourth, receiving the full precepts (*upasampadā*) through the remaining strength of one's great undertaking;

and fifth, the profound influence [of the Dharma], which may be explained in terms of its profound mystery or interpreted according to the color of the robes—referring simply to the color black (*śyāma*).
The latter phrase refers to the propagation of the Vinaya; "one whose will resides therein" means that this is what one has taken as the primary focus of one’s life, such as filial piety.
The Sūtra states: "My will lies in the *Chunqiu*, my practice in the *Xiaojing*; the pure model is the precepts (*śīla*).

Furthermore, the Fourth Reliance among the Patriarchs manifested in human form throughout the three periods of time to uphold and establish the Vinaya vehicle, specializing in the propagation of the study of the precepts. Thus, the commentary notes:
"I relied on the Master for instruction, reciting the commentary twenty times over a period of six years," and so forth.

The first four lines below clarify the period of his studies. It is said that the Master traveled extensively throughout the capital region during his worldly ministry, not remaining in a single location.
"Vouchsafing his heart" means he maintained proper etiquette while relying on a teacher; "requesting instruction" means seeking out the meanings of the texts.
This period lasted twelve years, and since his ministry began immediately thereafter, it amounts to twenty-four years. "Successively following" refers to the continuous succession of these years.
Alternatively, "carrying on" (*zǎijì*) may be a general term for "years," and "years" must refer to a single year, following in succession in this manner.

As for the two lines below, they are threefold praises of the *Prātimokṣa* (the Fundamental Code). The upper line refers to each time one consults it; the lower line praises its textual meaning as being profound and recondite.
"Kǎi" (慨) is simply a term for praise.
The first section is divided into two parts. First, the narration of the four departures and the seeking of differences. The first two phrases describe the time:

"Zhen Guan" refers to the reign title of Emperor Taizong of Tang, during which twenty-odd years were attained. The subsequent phrase indicates the location: "Mountains" (*yue*) refers to mountain ranges;

"Rivers and Marshes" (*shu*) refers to streams and waterways; these together form a general designation for the terrain traversed. This means crossing over rivers and land. "Bao" (薄) means "briefly" or "slightly. Alternatively, it may refer to the northwest.
He then took the character "Yue" (岳) because there were many mountains and lands; traveling to the southeast, he used the character "Du" (瀆) because there were many rivers, streams, and marshes.

The commentary on the *Shu* states: "In the fourth year of the Zhenguan era, he observed the transformations beyond [the mundane] and traveled north through Bingzhou and Jin, reaching the territory of Wei.
The subsequent phrase, "visiting the Way," refers to requesting [discussions] to evaluate the relative merits of the various Buddhist teachings.

The following section clarifies the distinction between the two types of teachers, the ignorant and the wise. First, regarding the ignorant teacher, the initial four lines illustrate his lack of understanding regarding the core intent of the teachings.

The first two lines refer to those who, in their debates, become muddled and confused; "far-reaching" refers to being completely bewildered by the great meaning. The latter two lines concern forgetting the foundation:
since the very basis of propagating the Vinaya lies solely in its practical application, and although this has been transmitted and expounded since antiquity, most do not know it—only I [do].
The intention behind the title of the *Shōshū Honjō Jisshō Shō* (A Record of the Founding of Our School Based on the Spontaneous Enlightenment of the Patriarchs) is evident therein;

thus, the preface to the *Shō* states: "As for the manifestation of worldly practices, those who follow the established models have not one in a hundred who grasp them. Furthermore, the preface to the *Sō* states:

"As for the performance of rituals, I have yet seen where they find their ultimate refuge. Is this not a discussion regarding how the transmission and maintenance [of the tradition] has been unclear since ancient times?
There are those who claim that because words are empty and obstructive, there is no application of them to phenomena, and thus they completely forget the fundamental purpose of the teachings.

Next, the section on "slander" clarifies the neglect and superficiality of study; the first four lines describe shallow learning. Of these, the first two lines mean that the name does not accord with reality.
Regarding the "seven names," these refer to the names of the five categories and seven groups [of offenses]; one must be able to recognize and master even a single character of their headings.
This refers to the Vinaya Master (*vinayadhara*). The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "One who skillfully understands a single character is called a Vinaya Master.

The latter two phrases refer to study that does not reach the ultimate principle, while the former phrase refers to the pursuit of names and marks (*nāma-lakṣaṇa*). The practice and concealment [of the Dharma] signify the meaning of the rise and fall, as well as the superiority and inferiority of the Vinaya teachings.
Therefore, the Preface to the *Shu-chao* says: "I have always regretted that the records left behind by the various masters of previous generations merely consist of commentaries on the treatises."

The *Fèilì Wèndá Yàocháo* (Essential Extracts of Questions and Answers on Abolition and Establishment) is this very work. The latter phrase means that one does not know where to turn for definitive correction; "the mind directed toward the Way" refers to this.

In the question below, the first two phrases describe the lack of scriptural basis; "ancient commentaries" refers to the various treatises, while "abolition and establishment" refers to the mutual discrepancies found among the various schools.

Regarding the acceptance or rejection of the latter two phrases: as there is no textual basis for them in the Vinaya, the first phrase is based on the "exhaustion of the subtle points" (*qióngqiào*), while the second phrase is a conjectural statement following from the former.

From here downward, the second section describes Master Zhì; the first two phrases praise his learning and understanding, meaning that his knowledge and experience were comprehensive and all-encompassing.
"Born with knowledge" refers to those endowed with innate intelligence; the *Analects* states: "Those who know by nature are the highest;

those who learn through study are next; those who learn after falling into distress are next again; those who fall into distress and yet do not learn—these are called the lowest. The latter two phrases condemn such teachers.
"Spiritual function" (*shen yòng*) refers to wisdom and strategy, which are said to be unreliable and thus not to be depended upon. "Emotional grasping" (*qíng qǔ*) refers to... [text fragmentary].
If one does not cultivate the orthodox teaching, the heavens will be alienated and their communication severed.
Regarding the first section of the "Clarifying the Middle" within the third [part], there are three subsections. First, the introduction to the purpose:

the two preceding lines mean that previous editions have been subject to increase or decrease and elaboration or abbreviation based on individual ingenuity, rather than conforming to the intent of the Patriarch. The following two lines state that [this version] follows the orthodox teaching.
When there is a principle to which one may turn for refuge, then contentious disputes and confused arguments are suddenly stilled.
Now, the following two sections demonstrate the literary form; first, the four lines clarify the sutra and its commentary. The first two lines describe the primary sutra:

the word "attempt" (*shi*) expresses a fear that there may be things not yet understood, which would deviate from the Buddha’s intent; it is not yet spoken with finality, representing the humility of one who composes a work based on what has been transmitted. "Based upon" (*yi*)... [text continues].

Regarding the Vinaya: since the original text of the precepts was scattered throughout the extensive Vinaya, I have now extracted the core rules from those texts and compiled them into this written work without any alteration;

thus it is said, "fully recorded. The following two lines clarify that the scriptural text follows the Buddha’s own explanations, as each individual precept was explained by the Buddha himself, and my current commentary strictly adheres to his words. The final four lines [serve to] collate the text.

The first two lines differ from the above in that they describe the ancient version as having the same number of fascicles as the current text; however, the three-fascicle version of the current text is merely a later division.

Alternatively, it may be that there was an ancient transcription in clerical script (*lìwén*), and the current text, following the matters of the Vinaya, may be identical to it. The final two lines describe the present [work]:
while the commentary makes the characteristics of the precepts (*śīla-lakṣaṇa*) clear, this differs from the ancients who failed to distinguish these characteristics.

The first part, "May it further clarify the benefits for the three [levels of practitioners]," is divided into two sections. First, the "Direct Clarification" consists of the initial two lines, which universally apply to the three faculties.

The upper line concerns the length of time one has studied, while the lower line refers to whether the faculties are sharp or dull. The subsequent two lines refer to the three grades of understanding: the superior grade clearly knows both the matters and the transgressions; the middle grade, although the words... (the text continues).

*Excerpts from the Vinaya* (Shichao), in the section on "Observance and Transgression," clarifies the three types of those who uphold the *vinaya*. The superior type is one who recognizes both the matters and the transgressions; the middle type... Furthermore, regarding those who recognize their transgression but harbor doubts about the specific offense, or those of inferior grade who are confused about both the matter and the transgression—this refers to being deluded regarding the teachings, resulting in the commission of two offenses:
"lack of training" and "ignorance. Because these do not constitute a violation of the fundamental precepts, they are called "refined upholders of the Vinaya.
Thus, one whose understanding and practice are both thorough and whose mastery of what is permitted and prohibited is brilliant and precise is a teacher who transforms others through the Vinaya.
Since this is the root of the study of the Buddha-dharma, the *Chao* states: "While the Great Master was in the world, he especially propagated this scripture.
The preceding phrase refers to the various previous versions mentioned above, while the subsequent phrase means that it is for the sake of inexhaustible benefit.

The next section is divided into three parts. First, the introduction of the intent: the first two phrases cite ancient views, noting that many have erroneously claimed that each precept has its own distinct origin story (*nidāna*).
This is because, within the Vinaya, every established precept possesses characteristics such as the origin, the location, the offender, and the circumstances of the offense;

if these are not clarified according to the Vinaya, room is left for false assertions. The final two phrases demonstrate the necessity of such clarification, meaning one must rely upon the formal teaching.
When explained in detail, matters return to the examination of reality.
Therefore, the following section correctly demonstrates the categories of speech and provides citations;

since the conditions for the precepts are each distinct—for instance, the origin, the root text, and the transgressions of the precept against sexual misconduct—the various characteristics are extensively analyzed and categorized in the commentary so that they do not become confused. Essential elements have been deleted and supplemented as follows:

Since that text is extensive, I have now merely extracted its essentials to assist with current ritual practices. Alternatively, because the text is so voluminous it cannot be recorded in its entirety, I have stated that I have "deleted the essentials.
Where there are omissions in the matters, they shall be supplemented by the underlying principle.
The three lower phrases clarify the preceding statement; that is, the textual lines set forth the subsequent phrase, which concerns the divergent paths of observance and transgression.
Within these two [sections], they are further divided into two parts. The first two phrases correctly demonstrate the benefits of the precepts.

Regarding the first phrase on self-benefit, "moistening the body" means that by relying on the teaching to uphold the precepts, one’s conduct in movement and stillness follows the restraints of the Vinaya, such that every action accords with the Dharma; thus, the Dharma moistens the body.
The *Jiaojie yixu* (Procedures for Instruction) states: "When the four modes of deportment lack the moisture of the Dharma, one is called a 'withered sentient being.
As for 'radiant virtue' (*guangde*), when majestic deportment and practice are perfected and applied in every situation, then virtuous beauty shines forth.

The *Chao* (Commentary) says: "Truly, without the Dharma there is no way to illuminate one's deportment; without the Way there is no way to manifest one's virtue. The second phrase refers to benefiting others. Regarding "protecting the Dharma" (*hufa*):

Since the maintenance of the Dharma in the final age relies solely upon the Sangha Jewel, and since transgressions fundamentally stem from a lack of discipline regarding the precepts, the Commentary states:

"In upholding the Three Jewels, the Sangha is primary; there is indeed a reason for this. Those who rectify the times find that in the era of the Final Dharma (*mofa*), those who realize the principles and attain the fruits [of the path] are few;

thus, they must rely on majestic deportment to solemnize others and the restraint of the precepts to purify themselves, so as to enable sentient beings to give rise to right views through observation of these outward signs.

Because it is good, it is called "explanation"; it involves the removal of defilements, receiving the precepts, and the sequential entry into the Path, culminating in the monastic community’s procedures for receiving repentance (*poṣadha*), the invitation (*pravāraṇā*), the establishment of legal rules, and the admonition between teacher and disciple, superior and subordinate.
This constitutes the fundamental framework of the Buddha-Dharma; its endurance for ten thousand generations is due to the power of the *vinaya*.
Thus, the *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* states: "The *Vinaya-piṭaka* is the life-span of the Buddha-Dharma; where the *Vinaya-piṭaka* abides, the Buddha-Dharma abides."

[The commentary] now abides [in its proper place]. On the verge of descending to the next section, there is a further entrustment regarding the circulation [of the text], consisting of the first two phrases. These mean: first, that the words and meanings are free from confusion;

the former phrase is entirely based on the Buddha’s own words and is thus fully reliable for trust. Second, that [this work] is far removed from the ancient masters, so that there shall be no deviation or error.

The following two lines explicitly demonstrate the intent of the transmission: "Bequeathing it to those who are free from outflows" (*anāsrava*) does not mean being solely concerned with one's own benefit.

This implies that how could one merely equip oneself alone? Alternatively, "free from outflows" may refer directly to the fruit of sainthood (*āryaphala*); "relieving those with whom one has a karmic affinity" expresses the intention to benefit others.

This means that because one has long possessed a superior affinity for the Patriarchs, if one now encounters them, one should provide universal relief. As Mencius said: [The Way is] "to nourish all things."

"In times of adversity, one perfects oneself; in times of success, one brings universal benefit to the world. This is because the Great Compassion that manifests its response is fundamentally intended to establish deeds and teachings for the sake of all living beings;
how could it be solely for the purpose of self-benefit?
Therefore, the final two lines serve as a conclusion to indicate that one must not act arbitrarily or assume authority on one's own initiative; they are words summarizing what has preceded.
*The Commentary on the Preface to the Four-Part Prātimokṣa Sūtra* (Concluded).
